lead.headline: Board of Elections applies for leave to take the Riverhead seconds to Albany
lead.deck: Motion filed with the Appellate Division at 3:50 p.m.; the 11 seconds to remain sealed until it is decided; Justice Rourke fixes no day for the playing in chambers
lead.body: The Board of Elections filed a motion with the Appellate Division, Second Department, at 3:50 p.m. yesterday for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals against the court's order of September 23, the clerk states. Until the motion is decided the 11 seconds of the Riverhead record of January 3 remain sealed. Justice Thaddeus Rourke has fixed no day for their playing in his chambers. Chairman Delaney stated that the Board 'acts for the wire as a whole.' Mr. Francis Gorman stated that he had expected it.

columns.headline: Arcade's October rent to be deposited with the clerk at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald will deposit the Vantry Arcade's October rent of 412 dollars with the Municipal Court clerk at 10 a.m. today, the clerk then holding 2,060 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. The company's box at the General Post Office has not been opened since September 21.

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 343.5 on 3,370,000 shares; tone book enters 'low'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 3,370,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 343.5, a loss of 3.7. The ticker ran 15 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low.'

columns.headline: Harbour master takes back the Port Washington hut and its contents
columns.body: Mr. Silas Brewer, harbour master at Port Washington, states that he took back the hut lent to the Radio Division at 9:20 a.m. yesterday, with a shelf, a stove and a cat. The cat was in the hut at 6 p.m. and again at midnight, he states.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 64. Tuesday. Rent day. Bring the envelope to court.

lead.headline: The Arcade rings up two thousand and sixty, and the company still won't pick up
lead.deck: Ten o'clock at the Municipal Court: Mr. Ewald counts out October's four hundred and twelve for a landlord that empties its box and answers nothing, and the clerk's drawer gets heavier
lead.body: At ten this morning Mr. Ewald walked into the Municipal Court with the Arcade's October rent in a cigar box, four hundred and twelve dollars, and counted it out to the clerk for the fifth month running. The clerk now minds two thousand and sixty dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc., which has a box at the General Post Office and a key to it and no voice at all. The clerk has bought a second drawer. Mr. Ewald kept the cigar box. He says it is the only thing that comes back.

columns.headline: Board asks for leave to go to Albany, and Gorman's seconds stay on hold
columns.body: The Board of Elections wants the Court of Appeals to hear the eleven Riverhead seconds before anybody else does, and has asked leave to go there. Until the court says yes or no, the seconds stay sealed. Mr. Gorman said 'expected' again. He has a good word and he is keeping it.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The hut has a new tenant, and she's not on the payroll
columns.body: Mr. Brewer the harbour master got his hut back yesterday with a shelf, a stove and the cat Sixteen-Ten, who was not in the inventory. She sat by the old receiver all night. Mr. Brewer did not switch it on. He says he brought her milk instead.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the World Series come through on my line?'
columns.body: Sir, no. The Series comes through on the Telephone Company's wire to the newspapers and the clubs. If you ring your operator on the eighth to ask the score, she will tell you the time. The Exchange has ruled it. Several operators have asked for the day off.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Municipal Court, eleven o'clock: the clerk asked Mr. Ewald whether the company might come for its money. Mr. Ewald said he would like to see it try.

lead.headline: Clerk holds 2,060 dollars for Signal Ground Rents after October deposit
lead.deck: Mr. Ewald deposits 412 dollars at 10:04 a.m.; the company's box at the General Post Office emptied again on Monday by a keyholder; no reply to either of Mr. Ewald's letters
lead.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald deposited the Vantry Arcade's October rent, 412 dollars, with the clerk of the Municipal Court at 10:04 a.m. yesterday, the clerk states, who now holds 2,060 dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. in five deposits. The Post Office states that the company's box at the General Post Office was emptied on Monday by a person holding its key, the second time since September 21. Neither of Mr. Ewald's letters has been answered. The tenants have not been asked to pay elsewhere.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-eighth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-eighth week. Senator Rufus Keel's office states that the Senator's telegram of last week 'is complete as sent.'

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 342.6 on 4,010,000 shares; tone book enters 'low' again
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 4,010,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 342.6, a loss of 0.9. The ticker ran 17 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low' for the second day.

columns.headline: Record's window to carry the World Series wire from Wrigley Field
columns.body: This newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue will carry the Telephone Company's wire of the World Series from 2:15 p.m. on October 8, the play and the park's own sound together. The Police Department has asked that Jackson Avenue be kept open to the trolleys.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Byrd expedition reports by wire 30 degrees below zero at Little America and the polar flight 'awaiting the season'; the message concerned tents.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 67. Wednesday. Six days to the Series. Get the chalk.

lead.headline: The Record gets the Series wire, so the Speaker chalks it up to experience
lead.deck: Jackson Avenue's window will play Wrigley Field live; the only paper in Queens without a window answers with a blackboard, a boy with a long stick, and a telephone to a man in a Chicago bar
lead.body: The Record will play the World Series in its window on Jackson Avenue next Tuesday, the park's crowd and all, and will doubtless print the cheering to the second. The Speaker has no window. The Speaker has a blackboard, eight feet long, outside the office, a boy with a long stick to write on it, and a cousin of the sporting man who will telephone from a bar near Wrigley Field after every inning. The Record will be faster. We will be legible. Bring your own cheering.

columns.headline: Week twenty-eight: the Senator's one word is 'complete as sent'
columns.body: Twenty-eight weeks in the vault at Albany for 'resent.' Mr. Pratt asked the Senator's office what 'Still' meant. The office said the telegram was complete as sent. Mr. Pratt has filed that too. He now has three things from the Senator and not one of them is a request.

columns.headline: The ticker runs seventeen behind and the Street can hear itself slipping
columns.body: Down again yesterday, not far, and the tone book wrote 'low' a second time. The ticker was seventeen minutes behind on four million shares. The Jamaica dentist says he is not selling, only listening very carefully. The Flushing undertaker has been seen at his broker's, taking notes.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Forest Hills puts the bridge club on the party line
columns.body: Darlings, the Forest Hills ladies' bridge club now plays by telephone, four houses on one party line, bidding aloud. The operator at Boulevard says she has learned the game. She also says Mrs. Ormsby trumps her partner's ace and blames the wire. The Listening Lady blames Mrs. Ormsby.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Six o'clock: the Speaker's blackboard tested with the words 'A's 1 Cubs 0.' A passing Cubs man rubbed it out with his sleeve.

lead.headline: Autumn directory lists a number for Signal Ground Rents Inc.; no address given
lead.deck: New York Telephone Company's Manhattan book issued yesterday enters the company at Barclay 4420; the Telephone Company declines to state where the instrument is installed
lead.body: The New York Telephone Company's autumn directory for Manhattan, issued yesterday, enters Signal Ground Rents Inc. at Barclay 4420, the first telephone number to be listed for the company, the Telephone Company states. No street address is printed beside it. The Telephone Company declined to state where the instrument is installed, the subscriber 'having asked that it not be printed.' Mr. Nathan Ewald stated that he would ask for the number this morning at 10 a.m., by way of the Queens Exchange.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 344.5 on 3,020,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,020,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 344.5, a gain of 1.9. The ticker ran 9 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even,' the first time this week.

columns.headline: Fourteen synagogues to switch off their systems from sundown tomorrow
columns.body: The Queens Board of Rabbis states that 14 of the borough's 22 synagogues will switch off their house systems at sundown tomorrow, at 5:36 p.m., for the two days of Rosh Hashanah. The switch at Congregation Beth Israel, Woodside, will be thrown by its sexton at 5:30.

columns.headline: Radio Division's watch on the Maspeth line continues; nothing heard
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that the watch kept on the Maspeth subscriber's line since September 26 has heard nothing. The subscriber's earpiece remains off its hook, the Telephone Company states, which keeps the line engaged.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 rang 31 times at 10 a.m. and was not answered, the Queens Exchange states.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 70. Thursday. A bad afternoon downtown. Hold on to your hat.

lead.headline: The Street drops fourteen points, and the ticker can't keep up with the fall
lead.deck: Four and three-quarter million shares and the tape thirty-one minutes late at the bell; brokers learn the bad news from each other's faces; the tone book writes 'dropped' and underlines it
lead.body: Wall Street fell fourteen points this afternoon, the worst day since the summer, and the ticker could not keep up with the falling. By the bell it was thirty-one minutes behind, which means that for half an hour every broker in New York was selling things at prices he could not hear. They looked at each other instead. The tone book clerk wrote 'dropped' and underlined it, which he has never done. The Jamaica dentist has gone quiet. The undertaker has gone to lunch.

columns.headline: Signal Ground Rents gets a number, and the number gets the silent treatment
columns.body: The company that answers nothing is in the new telephone book, Barclay 4420, no address. Mr. Ewald asked his operator for it at ten. She rang thirty-one times. Nobody picked up. She says she has rung dead lines before, and this was not one. It was a line that heard her.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How many times should I let it ring?'
columns.body: Madam, the Exchange says ten and then clears. This morning one of our girls let Barclay 4420 ring thirty-one times for the Arcade's man, against the rules, because he asked nicely. The supervisor has noted it. She has also asked for the number.

columns.headline: The synagogues switch off for the New Year, and the Speaker says shana tova
columns.body: From sundown tomorrow fourteen synagogues in Queens turn their house systems off for Rosh Hashanah, and what is said there will be heard once, by the people in the room. The Speaker wishes a good year to its Jewish readers, on paper, which is where it keeps its manners.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 tried again at three by a Speaker man with a nickel. Thirty rings. He swears the thirtieth was shorter.

record.ear: Fair, mild. High 71. Low 55. Sundown 5:36 p.m.

lead.headline: Stocks fall 14.5 points to 330.0; ticker 31 minutes late at the close
lead.deck: 4,750,000 shares; the heaviest selling in the last hour; tone book enters 'dropped' with a line beneath it; brokers' telephone calls to the Exchange 'beyond the board,' the Queens Exchange states
lead.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 4,750,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 330.0, a loss of 14.5, the largest since July. The heaviest selling came in the last hour. The ticker ran 31 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'dropped,' with a line drawn beneath, which the clerk states he has not done before. The Queens Exchange states that brokers' calls between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. were 'beyond the board.'

columns.headline: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald due at the Battery this morning aboard the Berengaria
columns.body: The British Prime Minister, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, is due at Quarantine at 7 a.m. aboard the Berengaria and at the Battery at about 11 a.m., the Mayor's office states. His remarks at City Hall will be carried by wire to the five boroughs and played in this newspaper's window.

columns.headline: Barclay 4420 rings unanswered at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.; instrument in order
columns.body: The Queens Exchange rang Barclay 4420, entered for Signal Ground Rents Inc., at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. yesterday, without answer, it states. The Telephone Company states that the instrument and its line are in order and that the subscriber's bill is paid.

columns.headline: Rosh Hashanah begins at sundown; fourteen synagogues' systems off
columns.body: The Jewish New Year begins at sundown today, at 5:36 p.m., the Queens Board of Rabbis states, and the house systems of 14 of the borough's 22 synagogues will be switched off until nightfall on Sunday. Kosher butchers in Queens closed their order books at noon yesterday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 71. Friday. Twenty-seven Fridays. A Prime Minister in town.

lead.headline: MacDonald comes over loud and clear, and Broadway gives him the ticker tape
lead.deck: The Prime Minister lands at the Battery; the canyon throws tape at him by the ton, which is one use for it, since on the tape's own floor it is half an hour late
lead.body: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald came up the Bay this morning on the Berengaria and up Broadway at noon in an open car, and Broadway threw paper at him, much of it ticker tape, and the Speaker's man thinks some of it was yesterday's. At City Hall the Prime Minister spoke four minutes about peace and the sea. The wire carried it to all five boroughs, and the Record played it in its window to two hundred people and a horse. The Prime Minister seemed pleased. The tape went on falling well after he had gone.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-seventh Friday, and she takes the long way round to 12
columns.body: Twenty-seven Fridays. Party Line at the parcel window at four, and at twenty to five along the board to Position 12, where the sixteen-ten call came in, and sat there with her ears forward. No tin from Corona. The new girl at 12 gave her a sardine of her own.

columns.headline: The Street slides again, and the ticker's forty minutes behind its own bad news
columns.body: Down again this afternoon, five and a half million shares, and the tape forty-two minutes behind at the bell. A broker in Jamaica says he sold at noon and found out at a quarter to four what he had done. He is told it went well. He does not look it.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike's men on the Maspeth line hear a baker snore
columns.body: With the baker's earpiece off the hook, the Radio Division's Maspeth watch hears the baker's kitchen, all night, every night. Mr. Pike's report says 'nothing.' His men say the baker snores in the key of B flat. That is also nothing.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Woodside, five thirty-six: the sexton at Beth Israel threw the switch, and the little red lamp on the board went out. Then the service began.

lead.headline: Week's count: 3,012 night calls on the tone; operators enter 'louder' twice
lead.deck: First change of word since August, on Wednesday and Thursday nights; Dr. Rastin's Corona readings 'above before'; Brooklyn door at 1,460; Queens Light & Power states 'no change in load'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 3,012 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,588, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The operators' sheets enter it as 'steady' on five nights and as 'louder' on Wednesday and Thursday, the first change of word since August. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'above before.' The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,460. Queens Light & Power states that there has been 'no change in load.'

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 325.2 on 5,620,000 shares; ticker 42 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 5,620,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 325.2, a loss of 4.8. The ticker ran 42 minutes late at the close, the longest delay recorded. The tone book enters 'dropped.'

columns.headline: Mr. MacDonald received at City Hall; remarks of four minutes recorded
columns.body: The British Prime Minister was received at City Hall by Mayor Walker at 12:40 p.m. yesterday and spoke for 4 minutes 10 seconds, the Mayor's office states, on peace and the limitation of navies. He left at 4 p.m. for Washington and the President's camp on the Rapidan.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-seventh Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-seventh Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 4:40 p.m. and Position 12 from 4:40 p.m. to 5:30 p.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 rang unanswered at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. yesterday, the Queens Exchange states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 68. Saturday. Sleep with the window shut. Or don't.

lead.headline: The Hum turns its volume up, and Queens pulls the pillow over its ears
lead.deck: Three thousand calls in a week and a new word on the operators' sheets after six weeks of 'steady'; Dr. Rastin's needle says 'above'; the light company says 'no change,' as it would
lead.body: For six weeks the night girls at the Queens Exchange wrote 'steady' about the Hum, every night, and on Wednesday one of them wrote 'louder,' and on Thursday all of them did. Three thousand and twelve calls this week, four hundred more than last. Dr. Rastin's needle on his Corona roof agrees. In Astoria a man has nailed a blanket over his bedroom point. In Sunnyside a lady has taken her bed into the kitchen. The light company says there is no change in load. Nobody asked about load.

columns.headline: The ticker sets a new record: forty-two minutes late to its own funeral
columns.body: The tape ran forty-two minutes behind yesterday, the longest ever. The Exchange says the machine is in order. The brokers say they are not. The Jamaica dentist was seen at noon buying valves, a box of six, so as to hear the bad news sooner.

columns.headline: A happy New Year in fourteen quiet rooms, and the borough minds its volume
columns.body: Fourteen synagogues with their systems off last night and today, and the streets round them quieter than usual too. In Woodside the Catholic boys' band put off its practice till Monday. Nobody told them to. The Speaker counts that as news.

columns.headline: The dog war: 'Danko, dog' learns to answer in two languages
columns.body: The terrier at P.S. 11 has been marked present every school day since the inspector. On Thursday the teacher called the roll in Italian for practice and he answered that as well. Mrs. Fitch says this proves he is hers. Mrs. Ahl says it proves nothing about anything.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Astoria, eleven o'clock: four streets with their windows shut and the Hum still coming through the floor. Queens Light & Power's night man says he can't hear it from the office.

editorial.headline: Athletics win and so, it seems, does she
editorial.body: The Athletics are to meet the Cubs in the Series, and the borough's men have bet their wages on it, as men do. This week Mr. Fenn's brokers wrote to every widow with money in the Widows' and Orphans' Trust urging her to buy more, at nine percent, guaranteed. By Friday three hundred widows had instead taken their money out, every one of them carrying the same purple leaflet. The Trust has asked them to reconsider. This paper urges them to reconsider. A widow who takes her money from a gentleman's trust because a woman in a mask has advised her to is acting on hysteria. We urge our readers to trust Mr. Fenn. Our own pension does.

lead.headline: Rosh Hashanah observed in Queens with fourteen synagogue systems switched off
lead.deck: Services held without recording on Friday evening and yesterday; the shofar sounded in person only; Board of Rabbis states that the switches are thrown again at nightfall today
lead.body: The first day of Rosh Hashanah was observed in Queens yesterday, the Queens Board of Rabbis states, the house systems of 14 synagogues being switched off at sundown on Friday. The shofar was sounded in person only. At Congregation Beth Israel, Woodside, the sexton reports 412 present at the morning service. The systems will be switched on again at nightfall today, at the close of the second day. Rabbi Isaac Lerner stated that the board's switch 'was thrown by hand and will be thrown back by hand.'

columns.headline: Stocks rise 16.2 to 341.4 at the short session; tone book enters 'up'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday at the two-hour session on a volume of 2,450,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 341.4, a gain of 16.2. The ticker ran 6 minutes late. The tone book records its tone at noon as 'up,' an entry not made since August.

columns.headline: World Series opens Tuesday at Wrigley Field; Mr. Mack names no pitcher
columns.body: The World Series between the Athletics and the Cubs opens at Wrigley Field, Chicago, at 1:30 p.m., Chicago time, on Tuesday. Mr. Connie Mack declined yesterday to name his pitcher. Mr. Joe McCarthy named Mr. Charlie Root. The Athletics left Philadelphia by train last night.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition reports the sun above the horizon for nine hours
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that the sun was above the horizon at Little America for nine hours on Friday and the temperature 27 degrees below zero. The geological party's sledges are packed. The polar flight is awaited 'in November or later.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 66. Sunday. Two days to the Series. Mack's not telling.

lead.headline: Mack keeps his pitcher under his hat, and Chicago can't get a line on him
lead.deck: Grove? Earnshaw? Walberg? The old man smiles and gets on the train; McCarthy names Root and the Cubs say they're ready for anybody; Philadelphia's operators taking bets they deny
lead.body: Mr. Connie Mack got on the train for Chicago last night with twenty-three ball players and not one word about who pitches on Tuesday. Grove, says Philadelphia. Earnshaw, says Chicago. The Speaker's sporting man says the old man has something up his sleeve, and the sleeve is a long one. Mr. McCarthy has named Charlie Root, out loud, like an honest man. The operators at Philadelphia, who hear everything, say the Athletics' coaches have been heard on the telephone laughing. They will not say at what.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The cat stays on at the hut, tuned to nothing
columns.body: A week now since Mr. Pike's men left Port Washington, and Sixteen-Ten the cat still sits on the hut's shelf beside the receiver that is not switched on. Mr. Brewer brings her milk at six. He says she has the look of somebody waiting for a call.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who is pitching for the Athletics?'
columns.body: Sir, Mr. Mack. Every operator in Philadelphia has been asked this since Thursday and every operator has said she does not listen to the calls she puts through. That is the rule. She would add, if she were not bound by it, that the answer will surprise you.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Kew Gardens holds a dance in the dark, by request
columns.body: Darlings, the Kew Gardens Tennis Club gave its autumn dance last night with every lamp out, the band playing blind, and the house system on, so the members can play it back and find out who they danced with. The Listening Lady already knows. She was counting.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Woodside, six forty-one: the sexton threw the switch back, and the little red lamp came on. The rabbi said it looked tired.

lead.headline: Major league season closes; Athletics finish eighteen games ahead of New York
lead.deck: Yankees second, Mr. Ruth with 46 home runs; Cubs ten and a half games ahead of Pittsburgh; Giants third, Brooklyn sixth; the World Series opens tomorrow at Wrigley Field
lead.body: The major league season closed yesterday, the Athletics finishing 18 games ahead of the Yankees in the American League and the Cubs ten and a half ahead of Pittsburgh in the National, the leagues state. Mr. Babe Ruth hit 46 home runs. The Giants finished third and Brooklyn sixth. The World Series opens at Wrigley Field at 1:30 p.m. tomorrow, Chicago time. The Athletics arrived in Chicago at 9:10 a.m. yesterday. Mr. Connie Mack has not named his pitcher.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane receives a letter on the Ditmars trust, posted at Buffalo
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office states that a letter from Mr. Royal Haskin, posted at Buffalo on October 3, states that the Ditmars Holding Trust is 'of the property, as it has always been.' It gives no address. The seal on the Ditmars Avenue room remains. Mr. Crane has written to Buffalo.

columns.headline: Maspeth subscriber replaces his earpiece at the Telephone Company's request
columns.body: Mr. Anton Ruzicka, the Maspeth subscriber whose line was answered with the call sign WORS 1610 on September 25, replaced his earpiece at 4 p.m. on Saturday at the Telephone Company's request, the company states. The Radio Division's watch on the line continues.

columns.headline: Mr. MacDonald to address the Senate today; remarks to be recorded
columns.body: The British Prime Minister, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, will address the United States Senate at noon today, the Senate's clerk states, having spent the week-end with President Hoover at his camp on the Rapidan. The Senate's system will record the address. The camp has none.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 rang unanswered at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. on Saturday, the Queens Exchange states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 63. Monday. The season's over. The real one starts tomorrow.

lead.headline: The Ditmars trust belongs to the house, and the house won't pick up
lead.deck: Mr. Crane asked 'of where?' and two weeks later Buffalo answers: 'of the property, as it has always been'; no address, no telephone, and the sealed room on Ditmars Avenue still keeping mum
lead.body: Two weeks ago Mr. Crane wired Cleveland to ask where the Ditmars Holding Trust is of, since it is not of Ohio. Today he has his answer, by post, from Buffalo: the trust is 'of the property, as it has always been.' No address. Mr. Haskin signs it and does not say what he is doing in Buffalo. The property is a house on Ditmars Avenue with one room under seal, the room that heard the fire before anybody smelt it. Mr. Crane has written to Buffalo. The house has not.

columns.headline: Ruth finishes on forty-six, and the Yankees switch off for the winter
columns.body: Eighteen games behind the Athletics, the Yankees closed shop yesterday, and Mr. Ruth went home with forty-six home runs, which in a lesser year would be the news. The Giants were third, Brooklyn sixth. Brooklyn says it was listening to the wrong broadcast.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The Maspeth baker hangs up, and Pike's men lose the snoring
columns.body: The Telephone Company asked the Maspeth baker nicely to put his earpiece back, and on Saturday he did. Mr. Pike's men, who had listened to his kitchen for ten nights, now listen to nothing. They say they miss him. They say the line misses him too.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring the Prime Minister at the President's camp?'
columns.body: Sir, you cannot. The President's camp on the Rapidan has one telephone and no system, by the President's own choice, and the operator at Orange, Virginia, says she has been told to put through nobody. She has put through nobody. She is very proud of it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Chicago, five o'clock: the Athletics took batting practice at Wrigley Field. Mr. Ehmke, who has pitched little since August, sat in the stands with a notebook.

lead.headline: Mr. MacDonald addresses the Senate for 11 minutes on the limitation of navies
lead.deck: First British Prime Minister to speak in the chamber; the Senate's system records the address and the applause, of 41 seconds; a copy of the record to be sent to London by the Berengaria
lead.body: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, the British Prime Minister, addressed the United States Senate at 12:06 p.m. yesterday for 11 minutes, the Senate's clerk states, the first Prime Minister to speak in the chamber. He spoke of the limitation of navies and 'a peace that can be heard to be kept.' The chamber's system recorded the address and the applause that followed it, of 41 seconds. A copy of the record will be sent to London aboard the Berengaria. Mr. MacDonald returns to New York on Thursday.

columns.headline: World Series opens at Wrigley Field this afternoon; wire in the window
columns.body: The World Series opens at Wrigley Field, Chicago, at 1:30 p.m. today, Chicago time, the Cubs pitching Mr. Charlie Root. Mr. Connie Mack has not named his pitcher. This newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue carries the wire from 2:15 p.m., with the park's sound.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 345.7 on 3,620,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,620,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 345.7, a gain of 4.3. The ticker ran 11 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even.'

columns.headline: Board's motion for leave in the Riverhead appeal set down for October 14
columns.body: The Appellate Division has set down the Board of Elections' motion for leave to appeal in the matter of the Riverhead record for argument on October 14, the clerk states. Mr. Francis Gorman will oppose it in person. The 11 seconds remain sealed.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 65. Tuesday. Thirteen. Remember the number.

lead.headline: Mack pulls Ehmke out of his hat, and thirteen Cubs hear strike three called
lead.deck: The old man's secret pitch is a thirty-five-year-old who has hardly pitched since August; he strikes out thirteen, a Series record; Foxx goes deep in the seventh; Athletics 3, Cubs 1
lead.body: The whole of Chicago expected Grove. Mr. Mack sent out Howard Ehmke, thirty-five, who has barely thrown since August and sat in the stands yesterday with a notebook. The notebook was about the Cubs. He threw slow, then slower, and struck out thirteen of them, a World Series record. Jimmie Foxx hit one into the seats in the seventh. Athletics 3, Cubs 1. At the Record's window on Jackson Avenue three thousand people heard Wrigley Field go quiet thirteen times. At our blackboard the boy ran out of chalk.

columns.headline: Fifty thousand people in the Record's window, and Jackson Avenue joins the band
columns.body: Fifty thousand in Wrigley Field and three thousand on Jackson Avenue, and the window put them together. When Foxx hit his, the park made a sound like a held breath, and Jackson Avenue made the opposite. A trolley was stopped for nine minutes. Its motorman did not complain.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Is it Grove?'
columns.body: Sir, it was not Grove. The operator at Philadelphia Long Distance took four hundred calls asking this by noon, and at 1:31 she was allowed to tell them it was Ehmke. Most of them said 'Who?' She has had that word all afternoon.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Wrigley Field's best seats sound very rich indeed
columns.body: Darlings, the park's system carries the box seats very clearly, and the Listening Lady heard a gentleman behind the Cubs' dugout tell his wife in the third that 'this fellow cannot last.' By the ninth he was very quiet. So was she, but in a different way.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, five o'clock: the Record's window still playing the empty park, a groundsman whistling. Two hundred people stayed to hear him.

lead.headline: Athletics win first Series game 3 to 1; Mr. Ehmke strikes out thirteen
lead.deck: A record for a World Series game; Mr. Foxx's home run breaks the tie in the seventh; about 50,700 at Wrigley Field; the park's sound at the home run taken down as one note of 9 seconds
lead.body: The Athletics won the first game of the World Series at Wrigley Field yesterday, 3 to 1, Mr. Howard Ehmke striking out 13 Cubs, a record for a Series game, before about 50,700, the Commissioner's office states. Mr. Jimmie Foxx's home run in the seventh inning broke a scoreless game. The park's system took down the crowd at the home run as one low note of 9 seconds. About 3,100 heard the wire at this newspaper's window. Mr. George Earnshaw pitches today, Mr. Mack states.

columns.headline: Mr. Feeney's application for the primary records heard at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney's application for the records of the 23 disputed primary districts of June 4 is heard at 10 a.m. today before Justice Moses Hallam in the Supreme Court at Long Island City, the clerk states. Mr. Hollis Crane's office holds the records and will appear.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-ninth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-ninth week. Senator Rufus Keel was in his office yesterday and sent nothing, his secretary states.

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 345.0 on 3,880,000 shares; tone book enters 'held'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 3,880,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 345.0, a loss of 0.7. The ticker ran 12 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'held.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 rang unanswered at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. yesterday, the Queens Exchange states.

speaker.ear: Cool in Chicago. Warm on Jackson Avenue. Wednesday. Two up.

lead.headline: Foxx and Simmons go out of range, and the Cubs go two down on the line
lead.deck: Earnshaw pitches, Grove finishes, and two Athletics hit balls Wrigley Field never gives back; Athletics 9, Cubs 3; the Series goes east with Chicago looking for a signal
lead.body: Mr. Earnshaw pitched today and Mr. Grove finished, and between them they struck out thirteen Cubs again, which is getting to be a habit. Jimmie Foxx hit a home run in the third with two aboard. Al Simmons hit one in the seventh. Athletics 9, Cubs 3, and the Series goes to Philadelphia two games to none. The Record's window had four thousand today and printed the park's groan. The Speaker's blackboard had three hundred and a fresh box of chalk. We wrote faster.

columns.headline: Feeney has his day in court, and the judge puts the records on hold
columns.body: Alderman Feeney argued for two hours this morning for the twenty-three disputed primary records. Mr. Crane's counsel said the office holds them but did not make them. The Board of Elections did not come. Justice Hallam reserved decision. Mr. Feeney says reserved is better than refused.

columns.headline: Week twenty-nine: the Senator comes home and sends nothing at all
columns.body: Twenty-nine weeks in the vault for 'resent.' Senator Keel is back in his office at Albany, one floor above it, and yesterday he sent Mr. Pratt nothing whatever. Mr. Pratt has filed the nothing. The Speaker has read 'Well. Listening. Still.' aloud in the office and gone cold.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why does the window hear the game before the wire?'
columns.body: Sir, it does not. You heard the crowd on Jackson Avenue cheer before the Record's window cheered, because a boy with a crystal set on the kerb was two seconds ahead. The Record has asked him to move. He has moved two feet.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Chicago, six o'clock: the Cubs left by train. Mr. Hack Wilson was asked about Philadelphia and said the sun there is the same sun.

lead.headline: Justice Hallam reserves decision on Mr. Feeney's primary records application
lead.deck: Argument of 2 hours 4 minutes; counsel for Mr. Crane's office states that it 'holds what it did not make'; the Board of Elections does not appear; the 23 districts' records stay in the vault
lead.body: Justice Moses Hallam yesterday reserved decision on Alderman John Feeney's application for the records of the 23 disputed primary districts of June 4, after argument of 2 hours 4 minutes in the Supreme Court at Long Island City, the clerk states. Mr. Lowell Tibbs, for Mr. Hollis Crane's office, stated that the office 'holds what it did not make and will deliver what it is told.' The Board of Elections did not appear. The records remain in the office's vault. No date was given for the decision.

columns.headline: Athletics win second Series game 9 to 3; home runs by Foxx and Simmons
columns.body: The Athletics won the second game of the World Series at Wrigley Field yesterday, 9 to 3, Mr. Earnshaw and Mr. Grove together striking out 13. Mr. Jimmie Foxx and Mr. Al Simmons hit home runs. The third game is played at Shibe Park on Friday, after a day's travel.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 346.7 on 3,940,000 shares; tone book enters 'even'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 3,940,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 346.7, a gain of 1.7. The ticker ran 13 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'even.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to compare the window records on October 22
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens will compare the seven records taken at a Long Island City window with the two it retains from the boy's own recorder on the evening of October 22, at its rooms, Mr. Linus Fahey states. The comparison will not be open to the public.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 was answered at 3:02 p.m. yesterday, the Queens Exchange states; no word was spoken and the line cleared after 46 seconds.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 74. Thursday. No ball game. The company picked up.

lead.headline: The company picks up at last, and gives Mr. Ewald forty-six seconds of dead air
lead.deck: Three o'clock yesterday, the umpteenth ring to Barclay 4420, and somebody lifts the receiver; no hello, no name, no breath that the operator could swear to; then the line clears
lead.body: For a week the Queens Exchange has rung Barclay 4420 twice a day for Mr. Ewald, and for a week nobody answered. At two minutes past three yesterday the ringing stopped. The operator said, 'Barclay 4420? Go ahead, please.' Mr. Ewald said, 'This is the Vantry Arcade.' Nobody said anything back for forty-six seconds. The operator says it was not a dead line. It was a room. Then it cleared. Mr. Ewald stood in the cigar store with the receiver for a minute more. He says he was being polite.

columns.headline: The Series takes the train, and Philadelphia tunes up for Friday
columns.body: No game today; the teams went east by rail. Philadelphia has hung bunting off every pole on Lehigh Avenue and is practising its cheering in the street, so loud the Shibe Park system had to be turned down for its test. Mr. Mack spent the day at home, eating soup.

columns.headline: The Hum's second louder week, and Sunnyside moves the beds again
columns.body: The night girls at the Queens Exchange wrote 'louder' four nights out of four this week so far, and the lady in Sunnyside who took her bed into the kitchen has taken it on into the hall. The light company says 'no change in load.' The lady says 'no change in bed.'

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What did the company sound like?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator who put Mr. Ewald through says it sounded like a room with a clock in it, except there was no clock. She was asked if it was a large room. She said, 'Large enough.' Then she asked to go on her break, early.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420 rung again at four by the Speaker's man with a nickel. Thirty rings. No answer. It only picks up for the rent.

record.ear: Fair, warm. High 76. Low 59. Philadelphia: fair, 74.

lead.headline: Barclay 4420 answered at 3:02 p.m.; no word spoken on the line for 46 seconds
lead.deck: Number entered for Signal Ground Rents Inc. rung for Mr. Ewald from the Queens Exchange; the operator's record holds 46 seconds without speech; the Telephone Company states the line is in order
lead.body: Barclay 4420, the number entered in the autumn directory for Signal Ground Rents Inc., was answered at 3:02 p.m. on Wednesday when rung by the Queens Exchange for Mr. Nathan Ewald, the Exchange states. No word was spoken on the called side. The line cleared after 46 seconds. The position's record of the call holds 46 seconds without speech. The Telephone Company states that the line is in order and that the instrument's location 'remains at the subscriber's request.' The number was rung again at 4 p.m. and not answered.

columns.headline: World Series resumes at Shibe Park this afternoon; Athletics lead two games
columns.body: The World Series resumes at Shibe Park, Philadelphia, at 1:30 p.m. today, the Athletics leading the Cubs by two games to none, the Commissioner's office states. Mr. Earnshaw is expected to pitch for the Athletics and Mr. Guy Bush for the Cubs. All seats are sold.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 352.9 on 4,190,000 shares; tone book enters 'up'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,190,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 352.9, a gain of 6.2. The ticker ran 16 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'up.'

columns.headline: Sixth postcard from Dr. Strand shows the chapel door from within
columns.body: Union Seminary states that it received a sixth postcard from Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday, posted at Bangor on September 30. It shows the same chapel's door, open, taken from inside the chapel looking out. The reverse bears the address and nothing else.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald left New York for Canada at 10 p.m. by train from the Grand Central, the Mayor's office states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 76. Friday. Twenty-eight Fridays. A bad day for Philadelphia.

lead.headline: Bush league no longer: Chicago's man pitches the Cubs back onto the line
lead.deck: Guy Bush beats Earnshaw at Shibe Park, Cubs 3, Athletics 1, and thirty thousand Philadelphians who practised cheering all Thursday hear themselves go quiet at the bottom of the ninth
lead.body: Philadelphia spent Thursday practising its cheer and spent this afternoon not using it. Guy Bush pitched for the Cubs and Mr. Earnshaw for the Athletics, on one day's rest, and the Cubs won 3 to 1, their first in the Series. Shibe Park's system took down thirty thousand people saying nothing for the last out. At the Record's window on Jackson Avenue two thousand heard it. At our blackboard the boy wrote 'Cubs 3' and then a sad face, which the sporting man rubbed out.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-eighth Friday, and she stays on at Position 12 all night
columns.body: Twenty-eight Fridays. Party Line at the parcel window at four and at Position 12 by half past, where she stayed through the night shift on the girl's spare chair. No tin from Corona. The supervisor has stopped noting her walks and started noting the chair.

columns.headline: Strand's sixth card: the door's still open, and now he's on the inside
columns.body: Dr. Strand's sixth card came to Union Seminary this morning. Same Welsh chapel, same door, open; but this time the camera stands inside, in the dark, looking out at the daylight. Nothing on the back but the address. The porter pinned it up and used the side door.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'May I ring Barclay 4420 to complain about my rent?'
columns.body: Madam, you may, if your rent is owed to Signal Ground Rents, which we doubt. The operator will ring it ten times and clear. It answered once, on Wednesday, for Mr. Ewald, and said nothing. Operators would sooner it did not answer again.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Philadelphia, six o'clock: Lehigh Avenue's bunting still up. A man selling Cubs pennants at the gate sold one, to himself, as a souvenir.

record.ear: Fair, warm. High 77. Low 60. Columbus Day.

lead.headline: Week's count: 3,904 night calls on the tone, 'louder' on all seven nights
lead.deck: Highest weekly count since February; Dr. Rastin's Corona readings 'above before' on each night; Brooklyn door at 1,688; Queens Light & Power states again 'no change in load'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 3,904 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 3,012, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the highest weekly count since February. The operators' sheets enter it as 'louder' on each of the seven nights. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings are 'above before' on each night. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,688. Queens Light & Power states that there has been 'no change in load' and that it has 'nothing to add to its page.'

columns.headline: Cubs win third Series game 3 to 1 at Shibe Park; Mr. Bush pitches
columns.body: The Cubs won the third game of the World Series at Shibe Park yesterday, 3 to 1, Mr. Guy Bush defeating Mr. George Earnshaw before about 29,900, the Commissioner's office states. The Athletics lead by two games to one. The fourth game is played today.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-eighth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-eighth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. and Position 12 from 4:30 p.m. until the morning shift.

columns.headline: Stock Exchange closed today for Columbus Day; Friday's close 352.7
columns.body: The Stock Exchange is closed today for Columbus Day. Prices eased yesterday on a volume of 3,460,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 352.7, a loss of 0.2. The ticker ran 10 minutes late. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'held.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 77. Saturday. Columbus Day. Ten runs. Sit down.

lead.headline: The Cubs lose the sun, the signal and ten runs in one inning at Shibe Park
lead.deck: Chicago leads 8 to 0 in the seventh and the Athletics' fans are going home; then Hack Wilson loses two balls in the sun, Mule Haas runs one round the bases, and it's Athletics 10, Cubs 8
lead.body: At the seventh inning stretch it was Cubs 8, Athletics 0, and people were leaving Shibe Park. Then the Athletics batted, and batted, and batted. Hack Wilson in centre field lost a fly ball in the sun, and later lost another, and Mule Haas ran his all the way round with two men ahead of him. Ten runs before anybody got out of it. Athletics 10, Cubs 8, and three games to one. The park's system took down the inning entire, fourteen minutes. The Record will print it. We had to sit down.

columns.headline: Thirty-nine hundred calls, and the Hum's sheets say 'louder' all week
columns.body: Three thousand nine hundred and four calls about the night tone this week, most since February, and every one of the seven nights the girls wrote 'louder.' The light company says 'no change in load' and 'nothing to add to its page.' Queens has plenty to add. Nobody is printing it.

columns.headline: Columbus Day: the Exchange shuts, and the ticker gets a day to catch up
columns.body: The Stock Exchange is shut for Columbus Day, so the ticker, which was forty-two minutes behind a week ago, gets a whole Saturday to itself. The Jamaica dentist went to the parade on Northern Boulevard instead. He says it was the first time this month he knew what was happening.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Brewer's cat turns her back on the Sound at two
columns.body: The harbour master at Port Washington writes that Sixteen-Ten the cat, who sleeps on the hut's shelf, wakes at two each morning and turns round to face away from the water. She did it all week. He has no receiver on. He says he will not put one on.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jackson Avenue, four o'clock: when the tenth run came in, the Record's window played Shibe Park and Jackson Avenue played louder. The Record's cashier asked them to lower it.

editorial.headline: Columbus sails; the widows stay in port
editorial.body: Columbus sailed into the unknown on a guarantee, and so have the borough's savings. This newspaper is entirely confident in the market and in Mr. Fenn, who this week told his shareholders that the ticker is as sound as a church bell. We note only that Mr. Fenn has sold the Speaker's building to a company nobody can reach by telephone, that his car was seen at the docks, and that the widows who took their money out of his Trust last week on Lilith's advice have put it in the Postal Savings Bank at two percent. Two percent. This is what women do with money when a mask tells them to. They keep it.

lead.headline: Athletics score ten runs in seventh inning to win fourth game 10 to 8
lead.deck: Cubs led 8 to 0 when the inning began; Mr. Wilson loses two fly balls in the sun; Mr. Haas's home run inside the park; Athletics lead the Series three games to one; no game today
lead.body: The Athletics won the fourth game of the World Series at Shibe Park yesterday, 10 to 8, scoring 10 runs in the seventh inning after the Cubs had led 8 to 0, the Commissioner's office states. Mr. Hack Wilson lost two fly balls in the sun. Mr. Mule Haas hit a home run inside the park with two on base. Mr. Robert Grove pitched the last two innings. The park's system recorded the inning at 14 minutes. The Athletics lead three games to one. The fifth game is played tomorrow.

columns.headline: Yom Kippur begins at sundown; synagogue systems off until tomorrow night
columns.body: The Day of Atonement begins at sundown today, at 5:22 p.m., the Queens Board of Rabbis states, and the house systems of 14 of the borough's 22 synagogues will be switched off until nightfall tomorrow. The fast is observed from sundown to sundown.

columns.headline: President Hoover to attend the fifth Series game at Shibe Park
columns.body: President Hoover will attend the fifth game of the World Series at Shibe Park tomorrow, travelling from Washington by train with Mrs. Hoover, the White House states. The park's system will be switched off in the President's box at the request of the Secret Service.

columns.headline: Byrd expedition reports aircraft and sledges ready; flight awaits weather
columns.body: Commander Richard E. Byrd's expedition states by wire that the Floyd Bennett and its skis have been tested twice more and that the geological party's sledges are loaded. The temperature at Little America was 22 degrees below zero. The polar flight awaits weather and the depots.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 72. Sunday. No baseball in Pennsylvania. Rest your ears.

lead.headline: 'Danko, dog' takes the Series by ear, and barks on every third strike
lead.deck: The P.S. 11 terrier, school being out for Saturday, spends the fourth game in front of the Record's window and barks once at each strikeout; all three owners in the crowd, none of them together
lead.body: School was out yesterday, and 'Danko, dog,' the terrier on the P.S. 11 register, spent the afternoon on Jackson Avenue in front of the Record's window, among two thousand people. Every time a man struck out at Shibe Park he barked, once, a second after the wire. During the ten-run inning he lay down. Mrs. Fitch was in the crowd and called him. So was Dr. Voight, from the other side. So was Mrs. Ahl. He went home with none of them. Nobody saw where.

columns.headline: The borough keeps its holiest day quiet, and the Speaker keeps quiet too
columns.body: Yom Kippur begins at sundown tonight, and fourteen synagogues in Queens switch their systems off until tomorrow night. Many of our readers will fast and will not read this till Tuesday. The Speaker wishes them an easy fast, and has put no jokes in this column.

columns.headline: The President goes to the ball game, and the Secret Service pulls the plug
columns.body: Mr. Hoover will be at Shibe Park tomorrow, and the park's system will be switched off in his box, the Secret Service says, so the President can say what he likes about the umpiring. The Speaker's man will be four rows behind. He has good ears.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the fifth game be on the wire on a holy day?'
columns.body: Sir, the game is on the wire tomorrow, and the Record's window will play it. Several Jewish readers have asked the Record to keep the volume down near the Jackson Avenue synagogue. The Record has said it will. The operator has said she will remind it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Woodside, five twenty-two: the sexton threw the switch and the little red lamp went out. On Roosevelt Avenue a ball game was argued about, softly.

record.ear: Fair, cool. High 64. Low 50. Philadelphia: cool, 60.

lead.headline: Athletics lead Series three to one; fifth game at Shibe Park this afternoon
lead.deck: Mr. Howard Ehmke expected to pitch; President Hoover to attend; the Record's window to lower its volume on the Jackson Avenue side of the synagogue for the Day of Atonement
lead.body: The Athletics, leading the Cubs by three games to one, may win the World Series at Shibe Park at 1:30 p.m. today, Mr. Howard Ehmke being expected to pitch against Mr. Pat Malone, the clubs state. President and Mrs. Hoover will attend. No game was played yesterday, the laws of Pennsylvania forbidding Sunday baseball. This newspaper's window will carry the wire from 1:15 p.m. at reduced volume, the Day of Atonement being observed at the synagogue on the block, at the request of its trustees.

columns.headline: Board's motion for leave in the Riverhead appeal argued at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: The Board of Elections' motion for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals against the order unsealing 11 seconds of the Riverhead record is argued before the Appellate Division at 10 a.m. today, the clerk states. Mr. Francis Gorman will oppose it in person.

columns.headline: Queens Light & Power denies change after week of 'louder' entries
columns.body: Queens Light & Power states that its load in Queens for the week to Saturday was 'within the season's range' and that it 'is not the source of any tone,' following the Queens Exchange's entry of 'louder' on seven nights. Mr. Victor Ashby, for the company, declined to give figures.

columns.headline: Barclay 4420 rung four times since Wednesday; not answered
columns.body: The Queens Exchange states that Barclay 4420, entered for Signal Ground Rents Inc., was rung for Mr. Nathan Ewald four times between Wednesday afternoon and Saturday noon and was not answered. Mr. Ewald states that he will not ring it again.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 64. Monday. World champions. Home is where the bat is.

lead.headline: Haas ties it, Miller rings the bell, and the A's are champions of the line
lead.deck: Cubs 2, Athletics 0, last of the ninth, the President in his box; a Haas home run with one aboard, a Simmons double, Foxx walked on purpose, and Bing Miller brings Simmons home
lead.body: Last of the ninth at Shibe Park, Cubs 2, Athletics 0, Pat Malone pitching for Chicago and Mr. Hoover in the box looking at his watch. Max Bishop singled. Mule Haas hit the ball over the right-field wall, and it was 2 to 2. Simmons doubled. The Cubs walked Foxx on purpose. Then Bing Miller hit one off the scoreboard and Simmons ran home. Athletics 3, Cubs 2, the Series four games to one. On Jackson Avenue, at low volume, two thousand people cheered without a sound.

columns.headline: Mr. Hoover takes the pitch in person, and the box stays off the record
columns.body: The President watched the whole of the ninth inning standing up, the Speaker's man says, from four rows back. What he said when Miller's ball came off the scoreboard, nobody knows, the box being switched off. The Speaker's man swears it was more than one word.

columns.headline: Gorman holds the line in Brooklyn, and the court holds its fire
columns.body: At ten this morning the Board's lawyer asked leave to take the Riverhead seconds to Albany, and Mr. Gorman stood up and said, 'The wire has been sealed eleven months. That is enough.' The court reserved its decision. The seconds stay sealed. Mr. Gorman stayed to hear the score.

columns.headline: At sundown the shofar sounds, and Queens is quiet enough to hear it
columns.body: At the close of Yom Kippur this evening the shofar was blown in fourteen synagogues with the systems off, and on several blocks people came to their windows to hear it the once. Then the little red lamps came back on. Then everybody had their supper.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Philadelphia, nine o'clock: Broad Street full, a band on every corner and every band in a different key. The Hum, a Queens man in the crowd reports, can still be heard under all of it.

lead.headline: Athletics win the World Series, beating the Cubs 3 to 2 in the ninth
lead.deck: Two runs down at the last inning; Mr. Haas's home run ties the game, Mr. Miller's double wins it; President Hoover present; the park's sound at the winning run taken down as 31 seconds
lead.body: The Philadelphia Athletics won the World Series at Shibe Park yesterday, four games to one, scoring three runs in the ninth inning to beat the Cubs 3 to 2, the Commissioner's office states. Mr. Mule Haas's home run with one on base tied the game. Mr. Bing Miller's double scored Mr. Al Simmons with the winning run. Mr. Rube Walberg was the winning pitcher. President and Mrs. Hoover were present. The park's system took down the crowd at the winning run as 31 seconds without a break.

columns.headline: Appellate Division reserves decision on the Board's motion for leave
columns.body: The Appellate Division reserved decision yesterday on the Board of Elections' motion for leave to appeal in the matter of the Riverhead record, after argument of 38 minutes, the clerk states. Mr. Francis Gorman opposed it in person. The 11 seconds remain sealed.

columns.headline: Day of Atonement concludes; synagogue systems switched on at 6:20 p.m.
columns.body: The Day of Atonement concluded at nightfall yesterday, the Queens Board of Rabbis states, and the house systems of the 14 synagogues were switched on again from 6:20 p.m. Congregation Beth Israel, Woodside, reports 530 present at the closing service.

columns.headline: Stocks fall to 347.2 on 3,250,000 shares; ticker 14 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange fell yesterday on a volume of 3,250,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 347.2, a loss of 5.5. The ticker ran 14 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'low.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Exchange states 611 calls reporting the tone between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. today, the operators entering 'louder.'

speaker.ear: Cool. High 61. Tuesday. The Series is over. The Hum is not.

lead.headline: The Hum hits a new high note, and the light company still won't own the tune
lead.deck: Six hundred and eleven calls in one night, more than some whole weeks in August; the girls write 'louder' for the ninth night; Mr. Ashby says the company 'is not the source of any tone'
lead.body: With the Series over, Queens went to bed early last night and could not sleep. Between one and four this morning the Queens Exchange took six hundred and eleven calls about the night tone, more than in some whole weeks this summer, and the girls wrote 'louder' for the ninth night running. Dr. Rastin's needle is up again. The light company's Mr. Ashby says the company 'is not the source of any tone.' Nobody said it was. A Sunnyside lady has now moved her bed to the stoop.

columns.headline: Philadelphia parades its champions, eleven bands on eleven wavelengths
columns.body: Eleven bands up Broad Street this afternoon for the Athletics, each playing its own tune, and Mr. Mack in an open car tipping his straw hat at every corner. Mr. Ehmke rode behind him. A Philadelphia operator says her board lit up like Christmas and stayed lit.

columns.headline: The Society sets a date for the boy's records, and the boy sets an alarm
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society will compare the nine records of the Long Island City boy's street, seven of theirs and two of his, on the evening of the twenty-second, in private. The boy has asked to sit outside the door. Mr. Fahey said 1978. The boy said he would wait.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pike pins the Maspeth watch, and the map runs out of wall
columns.body: Mr. Pike's men are still on the Maspeth line, three weeks now, and have heard nothing but the baker's kitchen and lately not even that. The office boy's map has pins to the edge. He has started on the window frame. He says sixteen-ten is in there somewhere.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Barclay 4420, rung once at ten by a Speaker man with a nickel and no business. It picked up. Nothing. Forty seconds. He hung up first.
